title: What makes a microservice truly "independently deployable" (its own codebase/pipeline, private database, backward-compatible contracts, no shared-library lockstep), and why is independent deployability — not size — the real test of whether you have microservices or a distributed monolith?
shortTitle: What makes a microservice truly independently deployable

s1_definition.profdef: A microservice is independently deployable when you can build, test, and release it to production on its own schedule without coordinating a simultaneous release of any other service. This requires four things: its own codebase and CI/CD pipeline, a private database that no other service touches, backward-compatible API and event contracts so old callers keep working during a rollout, and no shared-library lockstep where a version bump forces every service to redeploy together. Independent deployability, not line count or service size, is the real test. If two "services" must always ship together, you have a distributed monolith that carries network cost without the autonomy benefit.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine the Payment department and the Account department. They are truly independent only if the Payment department can renovate its counter on Monday without closing the Account department too. That means each has its own staff and procedures (codebase and pipeline), its own private ledger (database), a promise that old forms still work while new ones roll out (backward-compatible contracts), and no rule that says "if head office changes the stamp, every department must change on the same day" (no shared-library lockstep). If renovating one department always forces the other to shut too, they were never really separate departments.
s1_definition.oneliner: Independent deployability means own pipeline, private database, backward-compatible contracts, and no shared-library lockstep; if services must ship together, you have a distributed monolith, not microservices.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A microservice is independently deployable when you can build, test, and release it to production on its own schedule without coordinating a simultaneous release of any other service. This requires four things: its own codebase and CI/CD pipeline, a private database that no other service touches, backward-compatible API and event contracts so old callers keep working during a rollout, and no shared-library lockstep where a version bump forces every service to redeploy together. Independent deployability, not line count or service size, is the real test. If two "services" must always ship together, you have a distributed monolith that carries network cost without the autonomy benefit.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, imagine the Payment department and the Account department. They are truly independent only if the Payment department can renovate its counter on Monday without closing the Account department too. That means each has its own staff and procedures (codebase and pipeline), its own private ledger (database), a promise that old forms still work while new ones roll out (backward-compatible contracts), and no rule that says "if head office changes the stamp, every department must change on the same day" (no shared-library lockstep). If renovating one department always forces the other to shut too, they were never really separate departments.

**One line to remember:** Independent deployability means own pipeline, private database, backward-compatible contracts, and no shared-library lockstep; if services must ship together, you have a distributed monolith, not microservices.

sections.s2_technical:
Own codebase and pipeline is the first requirement. Each service lives in its own repository or clearly separated module with its own CI/CD pipeline, so a commit to the Payment Service triggers only the Payment Service's build, tests, and deploy. If a change to one service requires rebuilding and redeploying several services, the boundary is fake.

A private database is the second. The Payment Service owns its tables and no other service connects to them. The moment two services share a schema, a change to a column forces both to redeploy in lockstep, which destroys independence. If the Payment Service needs account data it calls the Account Service or keeps a local read model updated by consuming `account-events`, never a direct `SELECT` into the other service's tables.

Backward-compatible contracts are the third. During a rolling deploy, old and new versions of a service run at the same time, so a new version must not break old callers. You add fields instead of removing them, you keep old endpoints while introducing `/api/v2`, and for Kafka you evolve schemas additively with a registry. For example adding an optional `reference` field to `PaymentRequest` is safe because old clients simply omit it. The expand-and-contract pattern makes breaking changes safe: first expand to support both old and new, migrate all callers, then contract to remove the old.

No shared-library lockstep is the fourth. A shared library of DTOs or utilities is convenient until a change forces every service to upgrade and redeploy on the same day, which is lockstep. You avoid this by keeping shared libraries tiny and stable, versioning them so services upgrade on their own schedule, and preferring duplication of a small DTO over a coupling that forces coordinated releases. The senior-level point is that size is a distraction: a small service that must always ship with another is still a distributed monolith, while a larger service that releases on its own is a proper microservice. The real test is always "can I deploy this alone, right now, without a meeting?"
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India the Payment Service team wants to ship a fix on Friday. Problem 1 — a shared DTO library is bumped, and now the Account and Notification teams are told they must redeploy too or nothing works. This is exactly shared-library lockstep, and the fix is versioned, stable shared code so each service upgrades on its own schedule. Problem 2 — the new Payment Service version adds a `reference` field to its request, and there is a fear it will break the old mobile app mid-rollout. This is exactly where backward-compatible contracts matter: an added optional field is safe. Problem 3 — a junior engineer wrote a direct query into the accounts table to save a call, silently coupling the two services. This is exactly what a private database forbids.

The mini-project builds a tiny `DeploymentPipeline` that shows one service deploying alone, a `PaymentRequest` contract that evolves by adding an optional field while an old client still works, and a `SharedContracts` version check that detects lockstep. A runnable demo deploys the Payment Service independently, sends both an old-style and a new-style request to prove backward compatibility, and flags an attempted lockstep upgrade.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build ONLY this service (independent pipeline)
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Deploy this service alone, no coordination needed
java -jar target/independent-deploy-demo-1.0.0.jar

# Rolling deploy in Kubernetes (old + new pods coexist briefly)
kubectl set image deployment/payment-service payment=payment:2.3.0
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a request to deploy the Payment Service version 2.3.0, then an old-style and a new-style payment request, then two shared-library version checks.

Step 1: The deployment pipeline for the Payment Service builds, tests, and deploys version 2.3.0. No other pipeline is triggered. This proves the service releases on its own schedule.

Step 2: An old client sends a `PaymentRequest` with no `reference` field. Because the field is optional, the service accepts it and auto-generates a reference. The old client is not broken by the new version.

Step 3: A new client sends a `PaymentRequest` with `reference="RENT-OCT"`. The same service version accepts it and uses the provided reference. Both old and new requests coexist, which is exactly what a rolling deploy needs.

Step 4: The shared-library check compares versions 1.4.0 and 1.5.0. Only the minor number changed, so it is a compatible change and services can upgrade independently.

Step 5: The shared-library check compares 1.5.0 and 2.0.0. The major number changed, which signals a breaking change that would force every service to redeploy together. The demo flags this as lockstep, the anti-pattern that turns microservices into a distributed monolith.

```text
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:40 INFO === 1. Deploy Payment Service ALONE ===
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:40 INFO [payment-service] build + test
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:40 INFO [payment-service] deploy version 2.3.0 — no other service touched
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:40 INFO === 2. Backward-compatible contract (old + new clients) ===
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:40 INFO Processing 50000 from SAV2001 ref=AUTO-SAV2001
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:40 INFO Old client: ACCEPTED ref=AUTO-SAV2001
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:40 INFO Processing 50000 from SAV2001 ref=RENT-OCT
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:40 INFO New client: ACCEPTED ref=RENT-OCT
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:40 INFO === 3. Shared-library lockstep check ===
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:40 INFO Compatible: services can upgrade independently
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:40 SEVERE LOCKSTEP: major bump forces all services to redeploy
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Four pillars of independent deployability
    │
    ├─ 1. OWN PIPELINE
    │     commit → [payment-service CI] → deploy 2.3.0  (others untouched)
    │
    ├─ 2. PRIVATE DATABASE
    │     payments DB ← only Payment Service   (no cross-service SELECT)
    │
    ├─ 3. BACKWARD-COMPATIBLE CONTRACT
    │     old request {from, amount}        → ACCEPTED (ref auto)
    │     new request {from, amount, ref}   → ACCEPTED (ref=RENT-OCT)
    │     both coexist during rolling deploy
    │
    └─ 4. NO SHARED-LIBRARY LOCKSTEP
          1.4.0 → 1.5.0  minor → independent upgrade
          1.5.0 → 2.0.0  major → LOCKSTEP (distributed monolith smell)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Independent deployability means I can build, test, and release one service to production on its own schedule, without a meeting and without a coordinated release of any other service. I always stress that this, not the size of the service, is the real test of whether you have microservices or just a distributed monolith. A tiny service that must always ship alongside another is a distributed monolith; a larger service that releases on its own is a proper microservice.

Four things make it real. First, each service has its own codebase and its own CI/CD pipeline, so a commit to the Payment Service at National Bank of India triggers only the Payment Service's build and deploy. Second, each service has a private database that no other service touches; if the Payment Service needs account data it calls the Account Service or keeps a local read model updated from events, because the moment two services share a schema a column change forces both to redeploy together.

Third, contracts are backward compatible. During a rolling deploy, old and new versions run at the same time, so I make additive changes: I add an optional field rather than removing one, I keep the old endpoint while introducing a new version, and I evolve Kafka schemas additively through a registry. The expand-and-contract pattern lets me make even breaking changes safely by supporting both forms, migrating every caller, and only then removing the old. Fourth, there is no shared-library lockstep. I keep shared libraries tiny and versioned so each service upgrades on its own schedule, and I would rather duplicate a small DTO than introduce a dependency that forces everyone to redeploy on the same day.

The question I always come back to in an interview is simple: can I deploy this service alone, right now, without coordinating with another team? If the answer is yes, it is a microservice. If the answer is no, I have a distributed monolith that pays the network cost of microservices while keeping all the coupling of a monolith.
